title: Frequency Counting Patterns
summary: Counting occurrences with a hashmap to answer anagram, majority-element, and top-frequency questions in one pass, plus the bucket trick that turns Top-K into linear time.

slides.markdown:
A **frequency table** is a hashmap from value to count — the natural next step once you've mastered plain membership (a set) and complement lookup (a value-to-index map). Anywhere a question asks "how many times does X appear," "what's the most common element," or "are these two collections the same multiset," a frequency table is the answer.

The one-pass shape is always the same: `counts[x] = counts.get(x, 0) + 1` while scanning, then a second pass (or a smarter structure) reads the counts back out. What varies is what you do with the counts once you have them — compare two tables, find the max, or bucket by frequency for a Top-K query.

This topic covers that whole family: anagrams, majority element, Top-K, and the signature idea that reduces "are these the same, rearranged" to a single equality check.

slides.subTitle: A single pass
Comparing two frequency tables
When a sorted string or count-tuple means "the same"
slides.markdown:
Comparing two frequency tables works, but there's a related idea worth naming separately: reducing an item to a **canonical signature** so that "are these the same, rearranged" becomes a single equality check between signatures, not a table comparison.

For anagrams, two natural signatures exist: the **sorted string** itself (`"eat"` and `"tea"` both sort to `"aet"`), or a **count tuple** — a fixed-length tuple of 26 counts for lowercase letters, e.g. `(1,0,0,...,1,...,1)`. Sorting costs O(k log k) per string; a count tuple costs O(k) to build but O(26) or O(k) to compare and hash.

This signature idea is the seed of the next topic in this group — grouping items by a computed key is exactly "bucket every item under its signature," which is Group Anagrams rather than Valid Anagram.

slides.subTitle: Via frequency counting — and its O(1)-space alternative
slides.markdown:
Majority Element asks for the value appearing more than n/2 times, guaranteed to exist. The frequency-table answer is direct: build the table, return the key with the max count — O(n) time, O(k) space.

The senior-level follow-up an interviewer will ask: can you do it in O(1) extra space? Yes — **Boyer-Moore voting**. Keep a candidate and a counter; increment the counter when you see the candidate again, decrement otherwise, and swap candidates when the counter hits zero. Because a true majority element appears more than half the time, it always survives this cancellation process.

```python
def majority_element(nums):
    candidate, count = None, 0
    for x in nums:
        if count == 0:
            candidate = x
        count += 1 if x == candidate else -1
    return candidate
```

The trade-off to state out loud: Boyer-Moore only works because the problem *guarantees* a majority exists — without that guarantee you'd need a verification pass, putting you back at O(n) time but still O(1) space.

slides.subTitle: Counts feeding a bucket array indexed by frequency
slides.markdown:
Top-K Frequent Elements asks for the k most common values. After building a frequency table (O(n)), the naive next step is sorting values by count — O(k log k) — but there's a trick that gets the whole thing to O(n): **bucket sort by frequency**.

Since frequency can never exceed n, allocate an array of n+1 buckets, where `buckets[f]` holds every value whose count is exactly `f`. Placing each of the k distinct values into its bucket is O(k). Then walk the buckets from the highest frequency down, collecting values until you have k — total work bounded by n, since there are at most n buckets and at most n values across all of them.

<<< Image: a frequency table (value -> count) on the left feeding into a bucket array on the right, indexed 0 to n, where each bucket holds the values that share that exact count; an arrow scanning the bucket array from the highest index downward, collecting values into a Top-K result list >>>

slides.sectionTitle: Bucket-by-frequency vs a heap for Top-K
slides.subTitle: O(n) vs O(n log k)
slides.markdown:
| | Bucket sort by frequency | Min-heap of size k |
|---|---|---|
| Time | O(n) | O(n log k) |
| Space | O(n) for the bucket array | O(k) for the heap |
| Streaming input (k fixed, n unknown)? | Awkward — needs n known upfront to size buckets | Natural — heap caps at size k as data streams in |
| Simplicity | A bit more moving parts | Very direct: push, pop if size > k |

Bucket sort wins asymptotically and is the answer if asked for the fastest possible solution on a fixed array. A min-heap of size k wins in practice for **streaming** data, where n isn't known in advance and you can't size a bucket array upfront — you maintain the k largest counts seen so far, popping the smallest whenever the heap exceeds size k. Both start from the same frequency table; they differ only in how they extract the top k from it.

slides.sectionTitle: Re-scanning for a count you already have
slides.markdown:
A common mistake: building a frequency table, then calling `items.count(x)` or re-iterating the original collection to look up a count you already computed and stored.

```python
counts = build_counts(items)
for x in set(items):
    if items.count(x) > 1:      # re-scans the whole list — O(n) per call!
        ...
```

`items.count(x)` is itself an O(n) scan. Called inside a loop over distinct values, this silently reintroduces the O(n²) behavior the frequency table was built to avoid. The fix is to read the count you already stored: `if counts[x] > 1`.

This is the same class of bug as calling `list.contains()` inside a loop — a correct-looking O(n)-per-call operation, called somewhere it turns the whole algorithm quadratic. Once you've paid to build a table, use it; don't fall back to the collection it was built to replace.

slides.subTitle: Frequency counting plus an ordered second pass

slides.markdown:
A subtlety worth stating precisely in an interview: "O(1) space" for a frequency table is only true when the **alphabet is fixed and bounded**. Counting lowercase English letters needs at most 26 slots regardless of string length — genuinely O(1). Counting arbitrary Unicode strings, arbitrary integers, or arbitrary objects has no such bound — the table can grow with the number of *distinct* values, which is O(k) and, in the worst case where every element is unique, O(n).

Interviewers will sometimes phrase a constraint as "lowercase letters only" specifically to let you claim O(1) space — noticing and using that constraint is a small but real signal. Conversely, claiming O(1) space for a frequency table over an unconstrained input type is a correctness-of-analysis mistake, not just a style nitpick.

Signals a problem wants frequency counting: the words "anagram," "majority," "most/least frequent," "count of," or "how many times" appear, or the question secretly reduces to comparing two multisets.

The recipe: build the table in one O(n) pass, then choose the read-out that fits the question — a single lookup, an equality/subtraction between two tables, a max-by-value scan, or a bucket-by-frequency pass for Top-K.

The next topic pushes frequency counting one step further: instead of counting raw values, it counts occurrences of a **computed signature** derived from each item — the same one-pass-plus-map shape, aimed at grouping rather than counting.
